patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral hand and foot weakness and numbness for 3 years, slow progression, family told to see a specialist
patient.history_present_illness: Harold Watkins is a 56-year-old electrician with a 3-year history of progressive bilateral hand and foot weakness and sensory loss. He has had extensive prior workup attributed his neuropathy to 'mixed diabetic and toxic neuropathy from electrical work' — both of which his current neurologist is questioning. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 5 years ago (current HbA1c 7.8%) and his prior physicians attributed his neuropathy to this. He works as an industrial electrician but denies any significant solvent or heavy metal exposures confirmed by occupational health records. He notes that his father was 'basically in a wheelchair at 60 from leg weakness' though he never received a diagnosis. He has two adult children, one of whom (son, age 31) recently complained to his own physician about numb feet. He denies alcohol use. Over the past 6 months, he notes episodic carpal-tunnel-like pain at both wrists that he attributes to his job. He has been wearing bilateral wrist splints. A recent EMG at an outside institution was interpreted as 'length-dependent diabetic axonal neuropathy consistent with history.' He presents now because a podiatry colleague noticed extremely high arches on foot examination and referred him, stating 'this doesn't look like diabetic feet.' He also has prominent muscle wasting in his hands (interossei and thenar) and what he calls 'claw hands' that he attributes to grip fatigue from electrical work. He takes no immune-modulating medications.

specialized_test.impression: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG — uniformly slow demyelinating pattern. Motor conduction velocities uniformly slow throughout all tested nerves bilaterally (27–31 m/s), without focal areas of greater slowing, conduction block, or temporal dispersion. Sensory nerve action potentials reduced or absent bilaterally. Needle EMG: large-amplitude, long-duration, polyphasic motor unit potentials consistent with chronic reinnervation of long duration. Findings indicate a diffuse symmetric demyelinating polyneuropathy with electrophysiological features suggesting hereditary etiology. Clinical correlation recommended.

FOCUSED CARPAL TUNNEL NCS: Median palmar latency at wrist: 2.0 ms bilaterally. Median-ulnar palmar latency comparison: difference 0.1 ms (both equally slow — because of CMTX global demyelination, not carpal tunnel focal slowing). No median-specific focal slowing at carpal tunnel. Tinel's sign negative bilaterally. CONCLUSION: No carpal tunnel syndrome. Wrist pain was from CMTX-associated hand intrinsic weakness and wrist instability, not carpal tunnel entrapment. Bilateral wrist splints can be discontinued.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease X-linked type 1 (CMTX1) with superimposed diabetic axonal neuropathy
critical_actions: Re-review prior NCS velocity pattern — uniform slowing <30 m/s is CMT, not diabetic axonal
Obtain 3-generation family history — the 'diabetic neuropathy' label prevented this crucial inquiry
CMT genetic panel (PMP22 then GJB1) — confirm specific type for accurate genetic counseling
CSF protein to exclude CIDP (normal CSF confirms hereditary diagnosis)
Correct carpal tunnel misdiagnosis — wrist splints are unnecessary, important to stop inappropriate intervention
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute to diabetes alone — velocity pattern is diagnostic of hereditary demyelinating neuropathy
Do not prescribe IVIG for CIDP — CMTX1 does not respond to immunotherapy; normal CSF excludes CIDP
Never give vincristine if chemotherapy is required — vincristine causes acute fatal neuropathy in CMT
Do not continue carpal tunnel splints without confirming focal median slowing at wrist

differential.key_features: HbA1c 7.8% contributes superimposed axonal loss; diabetic neuropathy ALONE does not cause uniformly slow velocities <30 m/s, pes cavus, claw hands, 3-generation family history, or giant MUPs; diabetes is contributing, not primary
PMP22 duplication negative; GJB1 pathogenic variant found — CMTX1, not CMT1A
Normal CSF protein excludes CIDP; uniform symmetric slowing without conduction block or temporal dispersion argues against acquired demyelinating; family history and giant MUPs point to hereditary
Occupational health review negative for toxic exposures; childhood symptoms predated occupation; family history spans 3 generations

key_reasoning_points: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: Three compounding errors led to missed diagnosis — (1) diabetes HbA1c 7.8% caused anchoring, (2) prior NCS misread (amplitude noted, velocity overlooked), (3) family history never obtained
KEY CLUE: Velocity 28-31 m/s throughout all nerves = CMT1 range; diabetic axonal neuropathy shows amplitudes reduced with velocities >38 m/s
GIANT MUPs: Decades of chronic denervation-reinnervation — cannot be explained by 5-year diabetes history; implies childhood-onset neuropathy
PES CAVUS + CLAW HANDS + INVERTED CHAMPAGNE BOTTLE = hereditary neuropathy stigmata; NOT features of diabetic neuropathy
CMTX1 white matter changes on MRI are a distinguishing feature from CMT1A — clinically relevant for counseling about episodic encephalopathy risk
X-LINKED INHERITANCE: Father severely affected (hemizygous male), daughters are obligate carriers, sons of affected father do NOT inherit from father
FALSE CARPAL TUNNEL: Common misdiagnosis in CMT — hand weakness is from intrinsic wasting, not entrapment; NCS shows global slowing without wrist-focal median slowing
